anonymousReviews.rationale: Canonical continuity is insufficient to justify civilian conduct, but remains directly relevant to Copan’s claimed compatibility between divine love, scriptural authority, and severe judgment.
Rauser’s method does not fully discriminate moral error from difficult teaching, but he explicitly treats intuition as fallible and does not simply restate his conclusion as a premise.

Rauser risks letting a preferred moral conclusion control interpretation, yet calls intuition fallible and offers divine-versus-human intent as a substantive premise rather than assuming his conclusion.
The warning is developed chiefly against Boyd and transfers imperfectly to Rauser, yet canonical authority is relevant to the interpretive dispute rather than a diversion to an unrelated issue.
Copan’s criticism focuses mainly on Boyd and does not establish collapse for Rauser, but openly identifies Boyd and addresses a relevant neighboring hermeneutic.
New Testament severity does not establish the conquest’s moral permissibility, but it directly challenges a proposed contrast between divine love and judgment and therefore remains relevant evidence.
Varied New Testament judgments do not justify conquest means, yet directly answer the asserted contrast between loving Jesus and severe divine judgment.
Rauser cites scholars about dating uncertainty, but uses observations within a date-range comparison and reaches only a cautious evidential conclusion rather than treating status as decisive.
Rauser does not conclude Joshua is false because its date is unsettled; he limits the conclusion to reduced historical confidence and lower theological weight.
Rauser does not infer Joshua is false because its date is unsettled; he explicitly limits the inference to reduced historical confidence and theological weight.
Rauser concedes hyperbole lowers numbers and repeatedly calls the residual civilian count indeterminate, while arguing even reduced scale leaves a moral burden.
Rauser does not rely only on failure to prove civilians absent; he offers positive narrative indicators from Rahab’s family, Ai, and the cited less-mobile inhabitants.

The same source dependence is adequately captured by appeal to authority; the record does not separately establish a psychological tendency to overweight authorities beyond that argumentative reliance.

anonymousReviews.context: Hess has explored this for decades, and that is the only conclusion he has been able to reach.
anonymousReviews.rationale: Copan treats Hess’s decades of specialization and claimed exhaustive search as sufficient to establish the military-citadel classification, while the summarized grounds remain too compressed to demonstrate that civilians were excluded.
Copan stresses Hess’s expertise, but also reports archaeological considerations, drive-out priority, narrative survivors, and obedience language; authority status is not his sole support.
Rauser expressly preserves uncertainty about whether the civilian number was larger or smaller and argues that even residual intentional killing remains morally relevant, so he does not ignore scale.
Rauser notes no sparing directive but does not rely on silence alone; he adds Ai’s men-and-women description and sword-and-spear mechanics.
Rauser insufficiently establishes technical fit and intent, but supplies a convention definition, asserted acts, expulsion, and residential-school analogy rather than merely restating genocide.
Rauser incompletely applies a quoted genocide definition to cultural removal, but the defect is an unsupported legal bridge rather than a demonstrated shift in one key term’s meaning.
Rauser may overextend genocide doctrine to cultural-marker removal, but the source shows an explicit proposed application, not a covert mid-argument switch in a key term.
Copan openly identifies several meanings of herem and argues only that the word alone cannot prove extermination; he does not covertly switch meanings to secure his conclusion.
Copan openly argues herem has context-dependent senses and does not silently alternate meanings within one inference; his unresolved task is selecting the relevant conquest sense.

Copan offers the principled claim that additional contextual facts can override intuition, illustrated by Isaac; his failure to supply comparable conquest facts is incompleteness rather than an unprincipled exception.
Copan leaves conquest-specific overriding facts unspecified, but proposes a general rule that contextual revealed facts can defeat intuition and illustrates that same rule through Abraham.
Rauser’s conclusion is morally vivid and depends on contested premises, but he reasons from a stated Christological standard and concedes fallibility rather than judging solely by believability.
The vivid contrast invites judgment by moral plausibility, yet Rauser connects it to earlier civilian evidence and concedes intuition’s fallibility, so believability does not replace inference.
The appeal is to a proposed shared moral and Christological judgment, not to Rauser’s private experience or personal resonance as proof that the disputed historical inference is accurate.
The airplane differs from alleged direct targeting, but addresses whether innocent deaths can ever be morally permissible rather than diverting to an unrelated issue.

Copan articulates a general category of exceptional, morally sufficient circumstances and an airplane example; the analogy fails to bridge direct targeting, but the exception is not wholly unprincipled.
Copan does not develop conquest-specific necessity and safeguards, but his airplane example supplies a principled general distinction that preventing catastrophe can justify foreseen innocent deaths.
Rauser does not reject uncertain options in favor of a clearer familiar claim; he deliberately surveys multiple uncertain readings and declines to claim that one has been established.
Rauser expressly presents a survey and does not claim uncertainty proves an alternative true; the move establishes available Christian readings, not final historical correctness.

Rauser quotes Shepard to illustrate future openness rather than treating Shepard’s scholarly status as settling intrinsic wrongness, and the frozen critique keeps Shepard’s view separate from Copan’s.
Rauser treats civilian targeting as intrinsically wrong and analogizes it to assault; although this premise needs defense against exceptions, a contested moral premise is not automatically circular.
Another scholar’s future openness cannot establish Copan’s view and has limited relevance, but Rauser keeps it separate from his direct intrinsic-wrongness challenge.
